title: Orders and Ammunition
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 2 of 40
content:
Paladin Danse walked like the Commonwealth had offended him personally.

Not angrily. Anger wasted energy. He moved with the steady purpose of a man who believed every mile had an objective, every ruined building contained either a threat or useful technology, and every person traveling beside him should know which category they belonged to.

I spent the first twenty minutes to ArcJet trying not to become a third category called nuisance.

“Spacing,” he said without turning around.

I moved farther from him.

“Not that far.”

I moved closer.

He glanced back.

“Are you doing that deliberately?”

“Doing what?”

“Testing the limits of a simple instruction.”

“I’m calibrating.”

His helmet hid his face, but the silence had texture.

“Stay approximately six feet off my right flank.”

“There. A measurable standard. We’re learning.”

“Outstanding.”

The word should have sounded like praise.

Somehow he made it a warning.

The road out of Cambridge was cracked open by roots and old explosions. Skeletons of cars sat at angles where traffic had frozen two centuries ago. Danse paused at intersections before crossing, scanned windows before passing them, and never once let the barrel of his rifle drift toward me.

That last detail mattered more than it should have.

People in the Commonwealth liked to talk about trust as though it were a feeling. Usually it was geometry. Who I allowed at my back. Whose hand hovered near a weapon. Whether someone watched the doorway or watched my pockets.

Danse watched the doorways.

We encountered two mongrels near an overturned truck. He dropped one before I had raised my gun. I caught the second as it came around the rear axle.

“Good shot,” he said.

I looked at him.

“What?”

“I said it was a good shot.”

“I heard you. I’m just surprised praise is in the manual.”

He resumed walking.

“Competence should be recognized.”

“Do I get a medal?”

“No.”

“A sticker?”

“No.”

“What does the Brotherhood give for morale?”

“Purpose.”

I laughed before I could stop myself.

He turned again.

“You find that amusing?”

“A little.”

“Why?”

“Because that answer was the most Brotherhood answer you could possibly give.”

His pace slowed.

“You know much about us?”

“Enough to know you like old technology, big armor, and speeches about mankind.”

“That’s a crude description.”

“Is it inaccurate?”

A long pause.

“No.”

That almost-smile appeared in his voice this time.

ArcJet rose beyond a line of dead trees, all white concrete and shattered windows, the old corporate logo still clinging stubbornly above the entrance. Danse stopped at the edge of the parking lot.

“From here on, remain vigilant.”

“You think something’s inside?”

“I think assuming a ruin is empty is how people become part of the ruin.”

That was good advice.

I did not tell him so. He already had the posture of a man carrying more certainty than was comfortable.

Inside, the air was colder. Dust lay thick across the lobby except where something had disturbed it. Danse crouched near a footprint I would have missed entirely.

“Recent.”

“Human?”

“Possibly.”

He rose.

I noticed then how loudly his power armor moved indoors. Servos whined. Metal plates shifted. Each step landed with enough weight to shake grit from the ceiling.

“You ever try sneaking in that thing?”

“No.”

“That explains a lot.”

He looked at me.

“If stealth becomes necessary, you can go first.”

“See? Teamwork.”

“Don’t push it.”

We found bodies deeper in the facility.

Not old ones.

Men in dark clothing lay near a security door with clean burns through their torsos. The smell hit a second later: scorched fabric, heated metal, something unpleasantly sweet underneath.

Danse’s humor disappeared.

He knelt beside one corpse.

“Institute.”

I stared at the blackened wound.

“You know that how?”

“Energy signature. And these men weren’t carrying Brotherhood weapons.”

“Could be someone else with lasers.”

“It could.” He rose. “I don’t believe it is.”

There was something in the way he said Institute. Not fear exactly. Hatred with a strategic vocabulary.

We moved through a narrow corridor. A terminal blocked access to the next section.

Danse stood behind me while I worked.

At first I thought the awareness crawling between my shoulder blades was because I disliked anyone watching me type.

Then I realized he had positioned himself facing away.

He was covering the hall.

“You trust me with the terminal?” I asked.

“I trust you to tell me if you can’t open it.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.”

I glanced back.

His helmet was still pointed downrange.

“But I’m beginning to think you’re capable.”

The lock clicked.

“Careful, Paladin. That almost sounded like another compliment.”

“Open the door.”

I did.

The first synth stepped through before I had time to understand what I was looking at.

Its skin was white plastic. Its face was a collection of hard mechanical shapes pretending at a human arrangement. It raised a weapon.

Danse fired.

The corridor exploded into red light.

More came behind it.

“Contact front!”

I dropped behind the terminal station while laser fire carved glowing scars into the wall. Danse stood in the center of the corridor like the concept of cover was optional for anyone wearing a walking tank.

He shot with frightening calm.

I leaned out, fired twice, ducked back as a bolt snapped past my ear.

“Three on the left!” I shouted.

“I see them.”

“Then shoot them!”

“I am shooting them.”

One synth fell.

Then another.

The third pushed forward and Danse met it at arm’s length. He caught its gun against his forearm, twisted, and drove his armored shoulder through its chest hard enough to crack the torso casing.

For one stupid second I forgot to fire.

He looked over.

“Problem?”

“No.”

“You stopped shooting.”

“I was recalibrating.”

“Do it faster.”

I laughed, breathless, and put a round through the next synth’s head.

We cleared the corridor.

Afterward Danse inspected my shoulder where a laser had burned through the outer layer of my coat.

“I’m fine.”

“That’s not the same as uninjured.”

“It didn’t touch skin.”

His gloved fingers hovered near the damaged fabric without touching.

Then he pulled his hand back.

“Good.”

The word came out quieter than the others.

We continued deeper into ArcJet.

At the next stairwell, he stopped me with one arm across my path.

“Listen.”

I did.

Below us came the faint mechanical cadence of more synthetic feet.

Danse lowered his rifle.

“This facility is more heavily occupied than I anticipated.”

“So we leave?”

“No.”

Of course not.

His head turned toward me.

“You still have the option.”

That surprised me enough that I forgot to make a joke.

“You’re releasing me from duty?”

“You’re not under my command.”

“You’ve spent the last hour acting like I am.”

“That’s different.”

“How?”

Another pause.

“Habit.”

There was something unexpectedly honest about that.

I checked my magazine.

“I’m staying.”

Danse watched me for a long moment.

Then he nodded once.

“Good.”

Not outstanding.

Good.

For reasons I did not want to examine in the middle of an Institute-infested ruin, that felt better.

ArcJet’s parking lot offered a final stretch of open ground before the building swallowed us.

Danse used it to teach me hand signals.

He did not announce that this was what he was doing. He simply stopped, raised two fingers, pointed left, then stared at me until I did something.

I stared back.

He repeated the gesture.

“Is this a test?”

“Yes.”

“You could have mentioned there would be a test.”

“In combat, there is rarely advance notice.”

“That is a terrible educational philosophy.”

“Move left.”

“Oh.” I moved left. “See? Words.”

He ignored me and demonstrated the signals for stop, advance, enemy sighted, take cover, and regroup. I repeated each one until he was satisfied.

“Again,” he said.

I did them again.

“Faster.”

I did.

“Good.”

The approval landed with irritating force.

I covered it with sarcasm. “Still no sticker?”

“Your fixation on stickers is concerning.”

“You keep withholding them.”

A gust moved ash across the pavement between us.

Danse looked up at the broken ArcJet sign. When he spoke again, the humor had drained away.

“Once we’re inside, stay alert. The energy readings suggest active systems. That could mean automated defenses.”

“Or whoever turned them on.”

“Correct.”

His rifle came up into a ready position.

I watched the shift happen. The man who had almost joked with me disappeared behind training and objective and armor—not because the first version was false, I realized, but because this one was how he kept people alive.

“How many times have you done this?” I asked.

“Entered a pre-War facility?”

“Walked into someplace where you didn’t know what was waiting.”

“Enough.”

“That’s not a number.”

“No.”

He glanced at me.

“You don’t need to prove anything in there. If the situation exceeds your capabilities, withdraw.”

The concern was buried under phrasing sharp enough to pass inspection.

“You worried about me, Paladin?”

“I’m responsible for anyone operating under my command.”

“I’m under your command now?”

“For the duration of this mission.”

“Did I sign something?”

“No.”

“Then I’m calling it a partnership.”

His jaw worked once behind the open faceplate.

“You are extraordinarily difficult.”

“And yet useful.”

He looked at me for one long second.

“Yes,” he said. “You are.”

That one had no sarcasm in it.

I wished, suddenly and inconveniently, that it did.

Danse sealed his helmet and headed for the doors.

This time, when his fist came up, I stopped before he had to tell me.
